title: The sudden palpitations
label: Case 17
presentation: 35-year-old man with hypertension and anxiety. Palpitations started suddenly 15 minutes ago, with fatigue and shortness of breath but no chest pain.
question: What is your first management step in this stable patient with regular narrow-complex tachycardia?
options: IV diltiazem before identifying the rhythm
teaching: The rhythm is regular and narrow; a re-entrant SVT is likely. In a stable patient, try vagal maneuvers (preferably modified Valsalva), then adenosine when appropriate. Reassess stability continuously. Obtain a post-conversion 12-lead to look for pre-excitation.

title: The irregular tachycardia
label: Case 18
rhythm: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
presentation: 57-year-old man with hyperlipidemia and diabetes has had palpitations and shortness of breath for 72 hours. Sent from clinic for an abnormal ECG.
question: Which consideration most changes your management of this patient?
options: Duration of AF, hemodynamics, anticoagulation and stroke risk
Give adenosine to terminate the rhythm
Perform elective cardioversion without assessing stroke risk
Assume every irregular narrow-complex rhythm is MAT
teaching: Evaluate stability and causes of AF. In stable AF with RVR, individualize rate/rhythm strategy and anticoagulation assessment. With symptoms for 72 hours, do not casually cardiovert without considering thromboembolic precautions. Instability attributable to AF warrants urgent synchronized cardioversion.

title: The rate of 150 trap
label: Case 19
presentation: 44-year-old man with a prior “heart problem,” previous cardioversion, and prescribed rivaroxaban presents with palpitations.
question: A very regular narrow-complex rhythm around 150 bpm should make you particularly consider what?
teaching: Typical atrial flutter often has atrial activity near 300/min and 2:1 AV conduction, creating a ventricular rate around 150/min. Examine inferior leads and V1 for flutter activity. Evaluate adherence to anticoagulation, duration, stroke risk, and stability when choosing treatment.

title: The COPD exacerbation
label: Case 20
presentation: 73-year-old woman with extensive smoking history presents with dyspnea, increased sputum production, and multiple prior admissions for similar symptoms.
question: What is the highest-yield initial priority for this rhythm in this scenario?
options: Treat the underlying pulmonary illness; correct oxygenation and electrolyte abnormalities
Immediate synchronized cardioversion for any MAT
Anticoagulate all MAT patients as if they have atrial fibrillation
teaching: MAT features at least three P-wave morphologies with variable PP/PR intervals and an isoelectric baseline. Treat the underlying pulmonary disease and correct relevant hypoxemia, potassium and magnesium disturbances. Cardioversion generally does not terminate MAT.
